children: By Mayumi Honda and Naho Osawa / Yomiuri Shimbun Staff Writers

A drug pricing policy adopted by the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump is fueling fears that Japan's so-called drug-loss problem, in which pharmaceuticals used overseas are not available in the country, will grow more severe.
The Japanese government insists it will expand the domestic drug market to ensure people get the medicines they need. However, numerous challenges remain.

A most-favored-nation prescription drug pricing policy was rolled out in the United States in May last year. This policy states that the prices of prescription drugs covered by Medicare, which provides health insurance for elderly and other Americans, and Medicaid, which provides health insurance for low-income households, will be reduced to a level in line with the cheapest price paid in comparably developed nations such as Japan, Britain, France and Germany. Part of this policy came into operation this spring.
As a result, pharmaceutical companies are more hesitant to put their products on the Japanese market, where drug prices are low.
This situation has made Nagoya City University Specially Appointed Prof. Hiroji Iwata uneasy.

"A new medication for breast cancer was approved in December, but we still can't use it here," said Iwata, who has been involved in cancer treatment for many years. "This is probably the result of the U.S. policy."

In Japan, new drugs typically receive official government pricing and go on sale within three months of approval. However, Inluriyo, a new breast cancer drug, got approved almost nine months ago but has yet to hit the market.
A spokesperson for Eli Lilly Japan K.K., which produces and distributes Inluriyo, said, "Price negotiations with the government are continuing, but no details will be disclosed."
Iwata said: "Many patients could use this drug and have high expectations for it. I want this drug to quickly be made available for use."
Drugs cost 40% of U.S. prices

A survey by the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America found that prices of drugs at their time of launch in Japan were the cheapest among other advanced nations. In 2023, such drugs cost about 40% the price of those in the United States. Under Trump's most-favored-nation policy, if a pharmaceutical company releases a new drug on the Japanese market, that lower price would be referenced when setting the cap for the U.S. cost, thereby pushing down the price in the United States.

The Japanese market, in many cases, accounts for less than 10% of total sales by major European and U.S. pharmaceutical companies. By contrast, the U.S. market generates about 50% to 70% of sales. Lowering drug prices in their largest market would deliver a heavy blow to those companies.
Consequently, pharma companies could pause sales in Japan as they attempt to avoid cutting their drug prices in the United States.

Pascal Soriot, CEO of British pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca PLC, said any decrease in the company's profits could mean a loss of research and development funds needed to create the next new drug. Although Soriot said AstraZeneca wants to provide medicines to many patients, under the current conditions, the company might become unable to conduct clinical trials for and sell new drugs in Japan.

According to a July survey that the Japan Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association conducted with 16 member companies, including foreign-affiliated firms, 38% of respondents said the most-favored-nation policy "was already having an impact" and 56% said they "expected the policy would have an impact."

Health, Labor and Welfare Ministry data indicated that 86 medicines that had been approved overseas were unavailable in Japan as of March 2023. That figure had climbed by 28 more as of April this year, and there are concerns that this number could rise even further in the future.
Financial resources stretched

The Trump administration insists that American patients have been saddled with high drug prices that were used to fund the research and development of new drugs, and aims to reduce this burden. At the same time, the administration plans to make drug prices higher in other advanced nations, in a bid to have the burden shared more fairly.

Many observers believe the most-favored-nation price policy will remain in place even if a new U.S. administration takes office. In July, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said her government would definitely address this issue to ensure that the public and patients could quickly get access to innovative medicines. During next fiscal year's official drug price revisions, the government plans to consider taking certain steps such as reviewing the system to set prices for new medicines and the policy to keep drug prices low during the patent period.

Japan's annual national medical expenses are approaching 50 trillion yen. This cost is funded by taxes, social insurance premiums and patients themselves. In a bid to rein in the growth in medical expenses that are rising due to the nation's increasingly elderly population and advancements in medical care, the Japanese government has, through lowered drug prices, raised funds and reduced the burden shouldered by the public and patients. Changing this approach would necessitate finding new funding sources.

"Simply hiking drug prices would increase the burden shouldered by the public," said Waseda University Associate Prof. Kanetaka Maki, an expert on business administration. "But that defeats the purpose if it means that needed medicines become out of reach. To what extent should public health insurance cover medicines and treatment expenses? And who will pay? And how? The time has come for the entire nation to think about these questions."
